books.title: Blood Meridian, or, the Evening Redness in the West
books.author: Cormac McCarthy

review.body:
Recently re-read this as part of a book club with a buddy. Couple of quotes from the re-read:

“In the morning they crossed a bed of thunderstones clustered on that heath like the ossified eggs of some primal groundbird.”

“Beyond the fire it was cold and the night was clear and the stars were falling. The old hunter pulled his blanket about him. I wonder if there’s other worlds like this, he said. Or if this is the only one.”

—————————

And some notes/discussion on the ending sequence:

The little girl gone missing at the end, after her bear was killed, was it the judge? Seems related to the judge killing the idiot. 

The Judge preys on children throughout the novel (there are multiple hints and references to missing children whenever he appears). Whenever children disappear in proximity to him, violence follows. 

A child disappears.
The Judge remains.
The Judge dances.

He survives. The innocent does not.

The bear and the girl matter symbolically too.
- The bear = something wild, ancient, mythic.
- It’s reduced to spectacle.
- It’s shot for entertainment.

Civilization isn’t moral — it’s just another arena for violence. The girl disappearing right after the bear is killed suggests:

The spectacle continues.
The ritual of blood continues.
The Judge continues.

review.body:
Notes:
—————

Wishful fantasies of entire nations result in myth. Folk psychology. 

Being able to mask underlying desires and express them in a way that others gain pleasure from. Creatively mask them. Poetic subjectivity. 

All children eventually realize that their mother is certainly their mother (having they came from her body). But the father less certain. 

The dreaming of different parents. Those grander. Not as a matter of replacing them, but rather to exalt them. Reminiscing over happy times long past. Projected via fantasy. 

Vasari recounts that in his last hour of life, Leonardo Da Vinci reproached himself for having offended God and mankind by failing in his duty as artist. 

All childhood memories are fantasies. Like nations. When a nation is small and weak it does not think of recording its history. Only later, does it look back and recount its deeds. Re-tooled to serve later preoccupations. 

The relation between obsessional neurosis and the compulsive nature of trivial activities. 

Da Vinci loved his mother more than any other woman, thereby presumed homosexual.

review.body: The Vine had no jukebox but a real stereo continually playing tunes of alcoholic self-pity and sentimental divorce. “Nurse,” I sobbed. She poured doubles like an angel, right up to the lip of a cocktail glass, no measuring. “You have a lovely pitching arm.” You had to go down to them like a hummingbird over a blossom. I saw her much later, not too many years ago, and when I smiled she seemed to believe I was making advances. But it was only that I remembered. I’ll never forget you. Your husband will beat you with an extension cord and the bus will pull away leaving you standing there in tears, but you were my mother. - Denis Johnson (Jesus’ Son)

review.body:
Stylistically, this reminds me of Suttree. But thematically? The ending of Cities of the Plain comes to mind. I don’t know, this was very different than what I’ve come to expect from McCarthy through his previous 10 novels (that I’ve read at least). Yet, The Passenger is still fundamentally McCarthy. It’s funny, deeply philosophical, and the last chapter? McCarthy at his best. I think I’ve got 10 highlights from the final chapter alone. 

Excited for Stella Maris (and eagerly waiting for my friends to finish this one so we can discuss).

And it’s still, to date, the best book I’ve ever read.

Armory Blaine is eternal - as well as F Scott.
